title: Indian Green Card Holder Says He Would Not Move to the US on an H-1B Visa Today
excerpt: Mohamed Zeeshan, a Columbia-educated columnist living in Virginia, says the H-1B pathway has become too uncertain for Indian professionals — citing new fees, a wage-weighted lottery, and a decades-long green card backlog.
body:
• Mohamed Zeeshan, a 32-year-old Indian green card holder and Columbia University graduate, says in a Business Insider essay that he would not attempt the same move to the US today on an H-1B visa
  • The H-1B program now features a wage-weighted lottery, a contested $100,000 fee on certain petitions, and Indian nationals face decades-long green card backlogs
  • Immigration experts increasingly point Indian professionals toward EB-1A and EB-2 NIW self-petition routes as alternatives to the H-1B pathway

Mohamed Zeeshan, a 32-year-old Indian national who holds a green card and lives in Arlington, Virginia, says the immigration climate has shifted so dramatically that he would not attempt the same journey today on an H-1B visa. In an as-told-to essay published by Business Insider, Zeeshan — born in Indonesia to Indian parents because of his father's work — recounts how he moved to the United States on a green card, bypassing the H-1B route entirely.

Zeeshan, a Columbia University graduate and foreign affairs columnist who has written for The Diplomat, the Straits Times, and Deccan Herald, says the calculation for Indian professionals weighing a move to America has fundamentally changed. His perspective arrives at a moment when the H-1B program is undergoing its most sweeping overhaul in years, with new rules that add cost, reduce predictability, and narrow the path from temporary work visa to permanent residency.

A Program in Flux

The changes are substantial. Starting with the FY 2027 cap season, USCIS replaced its traditional random H-1B lottery with a wage-weighted selection system. Under a final rule published in December 2025 and effective February 2026, each registration now receives entries based on its Department of Labor wage level — four entries for Level IV positions, down to one entry for Level I. The statutory caps remain unchanged at 65,000 regular visas plus 20,000 for holders of US master's degrees.

According to Outlook Business, USCIS confirmed in July 2026 that it received 211,600 valid registrations for FY 2027, a 38.5 percent decline from the 343,981 submitted for FY 2026. The annual cap has been reached and there will be no second lottery this fiscal year.

On top of the lottery overhaul, a White House proclamation in September 2025 imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions filed for workers outside the US. The fee's legal status remains unsettled: a federal district court in Massachusetts struck it down on June 8, 2026, ruling it was a tax the president had no authority to impose. But three days later, the government appealed, and the same judge granted a temporary administrative stay reinstating the fee while the case proceeds. A separate court in Washington, D.C., reached the opposite conclusion, according to a Cairnwise analysis, raising the possibility that the question could reach the Supreme Court.

The Green Card Bottleneck

For Indian H-1B holders, the temporary visa is only half the challenge. The employment-based green card backlog for Indian nationals stretches decades, a reality that leaves many professionals in legal limbo — tied to a single employer, unable to change jobs freely, and facing the risk of deportation if they lose their position.

The American Immigration Lawyers Association noted in an April 2026 analysis that demand for H-1B visas continues to surpass the 85,000 available slots, and that "relying on a single lottery outcome puts operational progress at risk." The AILA analysis urged professionals to adopt a "permanent residency mindset" and consider EB-1A (Extraordinary Ability) and EB-2 NIW (National Interest Waiver) petitions as direct routes to green cards that bypass both the H-1B lottery and employer sponsorship requirements.

"Rather than viewing these options as secondary to the H-1B, they should be seen as direct ways to protect your ability to work and lead."

— AILA Blog, April 2026

Diaspora Calculus Shifts

Zeeshan's essay reflects a growing sentiment among the Indian diaspora. His path — securing a green card rather than entering the H-1B pipeline — is one that immigration lawyers are now recommending more frequently. The EB-1A allows self-sponsorship for professionals who have reached the top of their field, while the EB-2 NIW is designed for those whose work has potential national benefit, including founders in AI, biotechnology, and clean energy.

The shifting landscape also extends to students. According to The Indian Eye, proposed changes to F-1 visa rules could narrow the Day 1 CPT pathway that thousands of Indian graduates use after repeated H-1B lottery rejections. Immigration attorney Elizabeth Goldman warned that "there's no doubt about it that this is going to have a massive impact on the companies that are in desperate need of top talent," noting that foreign nationals make up a substantial portion of the US AI talent pool.

For Indian professionals already in the US on H-1B status, the wage-weighted lottery adds another layer of uncertainty. Positions offering lower wages now face significantly worse odds in the selection process, a change that disproportionately affects entry-level roles — which, according to Department of Homeland Security data cited by Fox News, accounted for 83 percent of H-1B visas petitioned for between 2020 and 2024.

What's Next

The legal battle over the $100,000 fee is expected to continue through 2026, with a potential Supreme Court showdown. Meanwhile, USCIS has not yet published final selection rates or detailed statistics for the FY 2027 cap season, with additional data expected in the coming weeks. Proposed restrictions on student visa pathways remain in the comment and rulemaking phase.

For Indian nationals weighing a move to the United States, Zeeshan's message is blunt: the pathway that worked for him — arriving with permanent residency already in hand — may be the only one that still makes practical sense in today's regulatory environment.
nri_angle: Indian professionals weighing a move to the US face a dramatically altered H-1B landscape, with new fees, wage-weighted selection, and green card backlogs reshaping the calculation.
author: Diaspora Desk
